source_text: Saginentur eiusmodi dulcibus conuiuae sui: et loca et tempora et inuitator ipsorum est. nostrae coenae, nostrae nuptiae nondum sunt. non possumus cum illis discumbere, quia nec illi nobiscum: uicibus disposita res est. nunc illi laetantur, nos conflictamur. saeculum, inquit, gaudebit, uos tristes eritis. lugeamus ergo, dum ethnici gaudent, ut, quum lugere coeperint, gaudeamus, ne pariter nunc gaudentes tunc quoque pariter lugeamus. delicatus es, Christiane, si et in saeculo uoluptatem concupiscis, immo nimium stultus, si hoc existimas uoluptatem. philosophi quidam hoc nomen quieti et tranquillitati dederunt, in ea gaudent, in ea auocantur, in ea etiam gloriantur. tu mihi metas et scaenam et puluerem et harenam suspiras. dicas uelim: non possumus uiuere sine uoluptate, qui mori cum uoluptate debemus. tnam quod, est aliud uotum nostrum quam quod et apostoli, exire de saeculo et recipi apud dominum? hic uoluptas, ubi et uotum.
thought_title: The Christian's feast is not yet
orientation: Tertullian is contrasting the present joy of pagans at the shows with the deferred joy of Christians, who should mourn now so they may rejoice later.
pass_a_gloss: Let his guests be fattened with such sweets: both the places and the times and the inviter are theirs. Our dinners, our weddings are not yet. We cannot recline at table with them, because neither do they with us: the matter is arranged by turns. Now they rejoice, we struggle. The world, he says, will rejoice, you will be sad. Let us mourn therefore, while pagans rejoice, so that, when they begin to mourn, we may rejoice, lest rejoicing now together we then also mourn together. You are delicate, Christian, if you also desire pleasure in the world, indeed too foolish, if you consider this pleasure. Certain philosophers gave this name to quiet and tranquility, in it they rejoice, in it they are diverted, in it they even glory. You sigh for turning posts and stage and dust and sand. I would like you to say: we cannot live without pleasure, we who ought to die with pleasure. For what else is our prayer than that also of the apostles, to depart from the world and be received with the Lord? Here is pleasure, where also the prayer is.

choices.why: The passive subjunctive expresses a concessive or permissive command; 'fattened' preserves the image of feeding guests richly, matching the preceding honeyed poison metaphor.

choices.english: the matter is arranged by turns
choices.why: Renders the idea of alternating fortunes between pagans and Christians; 'by turns' keeps the temporal alternation explicit.
rejected: the thing is set in alternation

choices.why: Direct address preserves the rhetorical jab; 'delicate' captures the sense of softness and self-indulgence.

choices.term: metas et scaenam et puluerem et harenam
choices.english: turning posts and stage and dust and sand
choices.why: Each noun names a concrete element of the shows: circus turning posts, theater stage, stadium dust, amphitheater sand; literal rendering keeps the fourfold enumeration.
rejected: racecourse and stage and dust and arena
turning posts and theater and dust and sand

choices.term: exire de saeculo et recipi apud dominum
choices.english: to depart from the world and be received with the Lord
choices.why: Literal rendering of the apostolic wish; 'with the Lord' preserves the sense of apud as being in the Lord's presence.
rejected: to leave the world and be welcomed by the Lord
to go out of the world and be taken to the Lord

pass_b_english: Let his guests be fattened on such sweets: the places, the times, and the host are all his. Our dinner, our wedding, has not yet come. We cannot recline at table with them, because they cannot with us; the matter is arranged by turns. Now they rejoice, we struggle. "The world," Christ says, "will rejoice; you will be sad" (John 16:20). Let us mourn, then, while the pagans rejoice, so that when they begin to mourn, we may rejoice, lest by rejoicing together now, we also mourn together then.

You are delicate, Christian, if you desire pleasure even in this world; indeed you are far too foolish if you think that is pleasure. Certain philosophers gave this name to rest and tranquility; in that they rejoice, in that they are diverted, in that they even boast. You sigh for turning posts and stage and dust and sand. I would have you say: we cannot live without pleasure, we who must die with pleasure. For what other wish do we have than the apostles'—to depart from the world and be received with the Lord? Where the wish is, there is the pleasure.

last_rejected.why: auocantur means “they are called,” not “they are diverted.”
last_rejected.ruling: auocantur from auocare means to be diverted/distracted; 'called away' is literal but 'diverted' is standard and correct.
metas in circus context with scaenam, puluerem, harenam means turning-posts/goals in arena; rendering is correct.

polish.changed: Identified Christ as the speaker of the Gospel quotation, clarified the contrast between pagan and Christian joy, and smoothed the sentence rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim and Scripture reference.

notes.quote: "The world," he says, "will rejoice; you will be sad"
notes.why: 'He says' without identifying the speaker; reader must infer Christ from the citation.
